subtitle: Read the text message every web request really is, and pull out the useful parts.
notes: This deck goes with exercise 1. By the end you should be able to explain what a request is made of and which Python tools split it apart.

slides.title: The big idea
slides.text:
When you open a website, your browser sends a short **text message** to a server: an **HTTP request**. One page needs many of them: one for the HTML, then more for each image, CSS and JavaScript file.

A backend's first job is to **read** that message. It's like cleaning data: one messy string in, tidy labelled fields out.
slides.notes: Link it to what you already know: you've split messy text columns into tidy fields in pandas. A request is one messy string that needs the same treatment.

slides.title: What a request looks like
slides.caption: This is the exact text the tests pass to your function as `raw`. `\r\n` means "new line".
slides.code:
raw = (
    "GET /api/tasks/?status=done&page=2 HTTP/1.1\r\n"   # request line
    "Host: localhost:8000\r\n"                          # headers...
    "Accept:   application/json  \r\n"
    "\r\n"                                              # blank line = end of head
)                                                        # body: empty for GET
slides.notes: You never type this yourself. The tests call parse_request(raw) and pass this text in.

terms.meaning: The verb: `GET` reads something, `POST` creates something.
The address that was asked for, like `/api/tasks/`.
Everything before / after the first blank line.
The name a function gives its input, like `raw`.

slides.title: What your function must return
slides.caption: `parse_request(raw)` turns the text into one dictionary:
slides.notes: Notice the header names are lower-case and the values have no extra spaces.

slides.title: Tool: partition splits once
slides.caption: `text.partition(sep)` is a **method**: it cuts at the **first** separator and gives back 3 pieces.
slides.code:
before, sep, after = "name: Ada Lovelace".partition(": ")
print(before)
print(after)

name, _, value = "Host: localhost:8000".partition(":")
print(value.strip())
slides.notes: Use _ for a piece you don't need. Because partition only splits once, the colon inside localhost:8000 is kept.

left.heading: text.split(sep)
bullets: Good for: splitting the head into lines

right.heading: text.partition(sep)
bullets: Good for: head vs body, and each header line

slides.title: Tools: urlsplit and parse_qsl
slides.caption: Both are **functions**: pass the text in brackets. `urlsplit` results use dots (`.path`), not `["path"]`.
slides.code:
from urllib.parse import parse_qsl, urlsplit

parts = urlsplit("/shop/search/?item=tea&size=large")
print(parts.path)
print(parts.query)
print(dict(parse_qsl(parts.query)))
slides.notes: Common mistakes from the chat: raw.urlsplit(...) (it's a function, not a method) and parts["path"] (use parts.path).

slides.title: Pattern: loop and build a dictionary
slides.caption: The same shape you need for the headers, on different data:
slides.notes: Start with an empty dict, and fill in one key per line inside the loop. Methods can be chained: key.strip().lower().

steps.text: Split `raw` into head and body at `"\r\n\r\n"` with `partition`
Split the head into lines; the first one is the request line
Split the request line into method, target and version
`urlsplit(target)` gives the path; `dict(parse_qsl(...))` gives the query
Loop over header lines and build `{lower-case name: stripped value}`
`is_safe_method`: upper-case the method, then check it's in `{"GET", "HEAD", "OPTIONS"}`

slides.title: Common mistakes
bullets: Forgetting `dict(...)` gives a list of pairs, not a dictionary
`NameError: raw is not defined` in the Console: make your own sample string first

slides.title: Where you'll use this
slides.text: A to-do app asks your server: `GET /api/tasks/?status=done`. Before your code can answer, something has to work out that the client wants to **read** tasks, only the **done** ones.
bullets: Django does this parsing for you: `request.method`, `request.path`, `request.GET`, `request.headers`, `request.body`
`is_safe_method` is how servers decide what anonymous visitors may do: reading is often allowed, changing is not
Knowing the raw format helps you debug APIs with browser dev tools or `curl`

slides.title: Check yourself
questions: What separates the head of a request from its body?
Why use `partition(":")` instead of `split(":")` for header lines?
Is `urlsplit` a function or a method? How do you read the path from its result?
Why do `GET` and `HEAD` count as safe, but `POST` doesn't?
